Roles with Rails: Contract-Preserving Role Evolution
in Multi-Agent Structured Reasoning

Ling-Yue Ge Affiliation: National Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Nanjing University, Suzhou, China*Corresponding author: guolz@lamda.nju.edu.cn    Lan-Zhe Guo Affiliation: National Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China
Abstract

Role-based LLM multi-agent systems need adaptive role pools, yet adapting such systems is not merely a matter of prompt optimization: roles often carry structural obligations, including capability coverage, message compatibility, validation, final-answer aggregation, and parser-compatible output protocols. Existing systems either fix the role inventory and lose adaptivity, or allow unconstrained generation to induce role drift, removing structurally necessary roles and breaking answer contracts. We formulate this as contract-preserving role evolution, requiring every committed edit to preserve five structural contracts (capability, communication, validation, aggregation, output protocol). We instantiate this formulation in Sero, a Self-Evolving Role Orchestration framework that evolves a typed role-card pool through credit-guided retrieval, a credit-ranked communication DAG with a protected terminal aggregator and conditional validator repair, and a contextual-bandit controller whose LLM-proposed edits are committed only when they preserve the contracts and improve task score. Experiments on real-world reasoning benchmarks across three LLM backbones confirm the value of contract-preserving role evolution.

1 Introduction

Role-based LLM multi-agent systems decompose reasoning across specialized agents such as planners, solvers, critics, validators, and aggregators, supporting task decomposition across specialist agents (Hong et al., 2024), multi-agent debate (Du et al., 2024), and graph-structured conversational coordination (Wu et al., 2023). Many deployed systems use a fixed role set or fixed interaction template and topology per task family. These fixed decompositions are stable precisely because their roles preserve capability, communication, validation, aggregation, and output-format contracts. Yet these same contracts make the role set fundamentally hard to adapt when the task distribution shifts.

Existing attempts to make role-based agents adaptive break this tension from only one side. Fixed-topology and pruning methods learn task-conditioned communication graphs or remove redundant agents and edges (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a), preserving task decomposition structure but cannot introduce new role capabilities. Dynamic role, prompt, and behavior adaptation methods rewrite roles or topologies, assign debate participants, or co-evolve agent behavior (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025), but unconstrained role updates could be unstable, removing useful roles, duplicating capabilities, or breaking answer protocols. Fig. 1 contrasts these regimes: frozen pools preserve contracts but add no roles; unconstrained editing adds roles but breaks contracts, leaving the challenge of doing both.

We formulate this problem as contract-preserving role evolution, in which a multi-agent system edits a reusable role pool while preserving the structural contracts required for coordination, checking, and final-answer production. An edit is valid only when it preserves five structural contracts. The capability contract keeps required expertise covered, preventing evolution from pruning the last role for a task family. The communication contract keeps intermediate states exchangeable under declared protocols, preventing incompatible or disconnected handoffs. The validation contract keeps error-detection or repair capacity reachable, preventing unchecked drafts from bypassing critique. The aggregation contract keeps a protected terminal role responsible for the final decision, preventing competing or missing final answers. The output-protocol contract keeps the final response compatible with the benchmark parser or application interface. Contract-preserving role evolution is therefore guarded editing over typed role cards, not unconstrained prompt search.

We realize contract-preserving role evolution as Sero (Self-Evolving Role Orchestration, Right of Fig. 1). Each agent is a typed role card carrying capability metadata, a communication protocol, a role type, and a protection flag, so contract checks operate on structured fields rather than raw prompts. Role-pool edits are framed as Add, Remove, or Noop decisions over a contextual-bandit controller, masked by the five contracts and committed only when they improve the task score under the same inference operator. At inference, Sero retrieves a small active team and routes it through a credit-ranked DAG terminating at a protected aggregator with optional validator repair, so each candidate pool is tested by the same executable contract check used during commitment. Our contributions are:

  • •

    Formalism. We define contract-preserving role evolution through five contracts and cast it as guarded editing over typed role cards.

  • •

    Framework. We propose Sero, a framework that admits an edit when it preserves five contracts and persists it only when it improves the task score under the same inference operator.

  • •

    Mechanism. Sero introduces typed role cards as contract unit, multi-scale credit for retrieval and removal, and a contract-masked, score-gated contextual-bandit controller.

  • •

    Evidence. Extensive experiments on three structured-reasoning benchmarks across three LLM backbones establish Sero’s superiority over single-agent and multi-agent baselines.

2 Related Work

Topology and Pruning.

LLM multi-agent systems decompose complex reasoning tasks across specialized agents and have increasingly been built around role-playing societies, software-engineering teams, debate-style frameworks, and tool-coordination platforms (Li et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023). Once a role inventory has been established, two adaptation strategies dominate existing designs. Topology methods learn task-conditioned communication graphs over a fixed inventory (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Leong et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Selection and pruning methods drop redundant agents or edges and assign per-agent credit during execution using difference rewards, leave-one-out effects, or Shapley-style estimates (Zhang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Wolpert and Tumer, 2001; Shapley, 2016; Nagpal et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025). These methods optimize how a role inventory communicates and which subset acts, yet leave the long-term composition of the inventory largely underexplored.

Dynamic Role and Prompt Adaptation.

Several mechanisms adapt a multi-agent system’s roles, prompts, or composition during a run. MetaGen evolves roles and topologies jointly (Wang et al., 2026), and online role assignment picks debate participants and models for role slots dynamically during an interaction (Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2023). Query-conditioned methods generate topologies and choose agents from an extensible pool (Li et al., 2026), and online prompt optimization updates agent prompts from feedback signals (Xia et al., 2026). Cooperative evolution updates role behavior through iterativeself-play in a fixed template (Chen et al., 2025). These methods improve adaptivity, but unconstrained updates to roles, prompts, or compositions can be unstable when they persist beyond a single decision, removing useful roles, duplicating capabilities, or breaking validation, aggregation, and output protocols. Sero instead treats role-set adaptation as contract-preserving role evolution, committing role-pool edits only when they preserve structural contracts and measurably improve the task score, and contrasts with the closest systems along six axes in Table 1.

3 Methodology: Sero

Problem Formulation.

We consider LLM multi-agent reasoning in which a persistent pool of typed roles collaborates to answer tasks drawn from a training distribution ptrainp_{\mathrm{train}}. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote this role pool and FF an inference operator that, given a task xx, assembles a task-conditioned active subset A⊆𝒫A\subseteq\mathcal{P} and produces an answer y^=F⁡(x,𝒫)\hat{y}=F(x;\mathcal{P}) scored by a benchmark scorer sx​(⋅)s_{x}(\cdot). We seek

𝒫⋆=arg⁡max𝒫​𝔼x∼ptrain​[sx​(F⁡(x,𝒫))],\mathcal{P}^{\star}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{P}}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{train}}}\!\bigl[s_{x}(F(x;\mathcal{P}))\bigr], (1)

subject to the requirement that every committed edit to 𝒫\mathcal{P} preserves the five structural contracts of contract-preserving role evolution (capability, communication, validation, aggregation, output protocol), so the pool remains executable under FF. Optimizing Eq. 1 by mutating prompts on per-task signals from sxs_{x} violates these contracts and yields pools that fail on non-trivial subsets despite high single-task scores. Throughout, e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) denotes a shared sentence encoder applied uniformly to task text, role-card prompts, and inference messages.

Overview.

Sero (Fig. 2) approaches Eq. 1 as a contextual-bandit Langford and Zhang (2007) problem in which edits to 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} are proposed freely across training steps and committed only when they both satisfy the five contracts and improve the task score under the same inference operator. Each component of Sero implements one face of this rule. Role cards make contracts explicit on each editable unit (§ 3.1). Credit estimates identify which roles can be safely retrieved, kept, or removed over time (§ 3.2). The inference operator FF acts as the executable contract test, retrieving a query-specific team, routing it through a credit-ranked DAG, and producing a protected answer with optional validator repair (§ 3.3). A guarded evolution loop binds proposals to contract-defined action masks and a score-gated commitment rule (§ 3.4).

3.1 Role Cards

Our editable unit is a typed role card rir_{i} whose fields map directly to the contract dimensions,

ri=⟨ni,pi,gi,fi,ℓi,Ti,νi,bi⟩.r_{i}=\langle n_{i},p_{i},g_{i},f_{i},\ell_{i},T_{i},\nu_{i},b_{i}\rangle. (2)

Tags gig_{i} and family fif_{i} encode capability, ℓi\ell_{i} specifies a communication protocol, νi∈{𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼,𝖲𝖾𝗍𝗎𝗉,𝖵𝖺𝗅,𝖠𝗀𝗀}\nu_{i}\in\{\mathsf{Spec},\mathsf{Setup},\mathsf{Val},\mathsf{Agg}\} is a role type (𝖲𝖾𝗍𝗎𝗉\mathsf{Setup} covers early task framing such as contract parsing), and bi∈{0,1}b_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether a role is structurally necessary, with bi=1b_{i}=1 for the terminal aggregator and required validators. The remaining fields nin_{i}, pip_{i}, TiT_{i} carry name, system prompt, and decoding temperature. Every commit must preserve all five contracts. (i) Capability. The pool retains at least one role per required capability family. (ii) Communication. The active team forms a DAG consistent with each role’s protocol ℓi\ell_{i}. (iii) Validation. A validator slot is reserved when post-aggregation repair is enabled. (iv) Aggregation. A protected terminal aggregator is appended outside the specialist budget. (v) Output protocol. raggr_{\mathrm{agg}}’s protocol enforces the benchmark-required answer format.

3.2 Credit Estimation

Credit is the evidence used to decide which roles can be safely retrieved, kept, or removed. Three signals provide it at complementary scales. Fast credit gives low-cost within-run attribution, precise leave-one-out credit calibrates whether a role was actually necessary on a task, and historical EMA credit prevents single-instance noise from causing unstable edits. Let mim_{i} denote the message produced by role rir_{i} in the current inference pass and e¯M=1|At|​∑ri∈Ate⁡(mi)\bar{e}_{M}=\tfrac{1}{|A_{t}|}\sum_{r_{i}\in A_{t}}e(m_{i}) the consensus embedding of active-role messages. Fast credit is a within-task proxy computable on every step, as

cifast=βcos(e(mi),ex)+(1−β)cos(e(mi),e¯M),c_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}}=\beta\cos(e(m_{i}),e_{x})+(1-\beta)\cos(e(m_{i}),\bar{e}_{M}), (3)

where ex=e⁡(x)e_{x}=e(x), the first term favors task alignment, and the second favors agreement with the active set. Validator fast credit is treated as a structured signal rather than a similarity score, and increases when validator feedback is adopted by a repair pass. Precise credit refines fast credit with periodic leave-one-out evaluation to approximate causal contribution under the current pool,

ϕ^i=sx​(F⁡(x,𝒫t,Ct))−sx​(F⁡(x,𝒫t∖{ri},Ct)),\hat{\phi}_{i}=s_{x}(F(x;\mathcal{P}_{t},C_{t}))-s_{x}(F(x;\mathcal{P}_{t}\setminus\{r_{i}\},C_{t})), (4)

and historical credit tracks longer-run value via the EMA update (Morales-Brotons et al., 2024), which can be formulated as:

c¯i:=(1−μ)​c¯i+μ​ϕ^i.\bar{c}_{i}\;\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\;(1-\mu)\,\bar{c}_{i}+\mu\,\hat{\phi}_{i}. (5)

New roles start with c¯i=0\bar{c}_{i}=0 and conservative update counts so exploration is possible without letting unevaluated roles dominate retrieval.

3.3 Inference Procedure

Inference is the executable contract test of the current role pool. The operator FF retrieves a compact team, routes information through protocol-compatible roles, produces a protected answer, and applies validator repair where needed. The same FF is applied at evaluation and during training, so the candidate-vs-current score difference reflects the behavior induced by the evaluated edit.

Active-Role Retrieval.

Candidate roles are ranked by a convex combination of semantic relevance and historical credit while always including the protected aggregator card raggr_{\mathrm{agg}} identified by νi=𝖠𝗀𝗀\nu_{i}=\mathsf{Agg}, which can be formulated as:

ρ(ri,x)=αcos(e(pi),ex)+(1−α)norm(c¯i),\rho(r_{i},x)=\alpha\cos(e(p_{i}),e_{x})+(1-\alpha)\,\mathrm{norm}(\bar{c}_{i}), (6)

where ex=e⁡(x)e_{x}=e(x) and norm⁡(⋅)\mathrm{norm}(\cdot) rescales EMA credit to [0,1][0,1] across the current pool. When validator passes are enabled, separate retrieval budgets are allocated for specialists and validators so critique does not compete with upstream reasoning roles, and raggr_{\mathrm{agg}} is appended after retrieval so the terminal contract is preserved. The retrieved set AtA_{t} becomes the vertex set for message scheduling.

Credit-Ranked DAG Construction.

Message scheduling uses a stage-aware order that prefers reliable contributors and reserves late positions for validation. Let AtA_{t} be the active set and Bt=At∖{ragg}B_{t}=A_{t}\setminus\{r_{\mathrm{agg}}\} the non-terminal roles, and define a lexicographic key as follows:

Ki=(κ⁡(νi),−cifast,i),ri≺rj⇔Ki<Kj,K_{i}=(\kappa(\nu_{i}),\,-c_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}},\,i),\qquad r_{i}\prec r_{j}\Leftrightarrow K_{i}<K_{j}, (7)

where κ⁡(𝖲𝖾𝗍𝗎𝗉)=−1\kappa(\mathsf{Setup})=-1, κ⁡(𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼)=0\kappa(\mathsf{Spec})=0, κ⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅)=1\kappa(\mathsf{Val})=1, and cifastc_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}} comes from Eq. 3. Edges are added greedily from earlier to later roles under fixed in-degree and out-degree caps, and every non-terminal role is additionally connected to raggr_{\mathrm{agg}} so the terminal aggregator always observes all upstream content even when intermediate coordination is sparse. The induced DAG is partitioned into dependency levels, roles at the same level are invoked in parallel, and each role receives the original task, upstream messages, and its role-card protocol. Algorithm 1 gives the full construction used in the experiments.

Aggregation and Validator Repair.

The terminal stage routes all messages to the protected aggregator raggr_{\mathrm{agg}} and produces the answer scored by sx​(⋅)s_{x}(\cdot). An optional validator intervenes on contract-risky drafts. If the validator flags an issue, raggr_{\mathrm{agg}} is re-invoked with the draft and validator feedback (Madaan et al., 2023), and the resulting output y^t\hat{y}_{t} feeds both the controller’s reward signal and the credit updates in Eqs. 3 and 5.

3.4 Guarded Evolution

We separate proposing from committing via three components, a controller policy πθ\pi_{\theta} selecting at=(ωt,zt)a_{t}=(\omega_{t},z_{t}) with ωt∈𝒪={Add,Remove,Noop}\omega_{t}\in\mathcal{O}=\{\textsc{Add},\textsc{Remove},\textsc{Noop}\} and ztz_{t} a target role for Remove, a candidate generator ℰ\mathcal{E} realizing ωt\omega_{t} as a typed candidate pool (𝒫t′,Ct′)(\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{t},C^{\prime}_{t}) under structural constraints, and a commitment rule Γ\Gamma deciding persistence from the candidate-vs-current score change

Rt=sx​(F⁡(xt,𝒫t′,Ct′))−sx​(F⁡(xt,𝒫t,Ct)),R_{t}=s_{x}\bigl(F(x_{t};\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{t},C^{\prime}_{t})\bigr)-s_{x}\bigl(F(x_{t};\mathcal{P}_{t},C_{t})\bigr), (8)

with Rt=0R_{t}=0 for Noop, invalid edits, or unchanged candidates. The training objective is J⁡(θ)=𝔼πθ​[∑t=1TRt]J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}R_{t}\right] under an action mask induced by structural invariants.

Controller.

The controller proposes edits, while the contract checker defines which proposals are admissible and the score gate decides which admissible proposals become persistent. A pre-decision inference pass with FF produces a provisional answer y^t\hat{y}_{t} and an active set At⊆𝒫tA_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{t}, which are summarized into the observation

ot=[e⁡(xt,y^t),e¯At,ψ⁡(Ct)],o_{t}=\bigl[e(x_{t},\hat{y}_{t}),\;\bar{e}_{A_{t}},\;\psi(C_{t})\bigr], (9)

where e⁡(xt,y^t)e(x_{t},\hat{y}_{t}) is the embedding of the task concatenated with answer, e¯At=1|At|​∑ri∈Ate⁡(pi)\bar{e}_{A_{t}}=\tfrac{1}{|A_{t}|}\sum_{r_{i}\in A_{t}}e(p_{i}) summarizes the assembled team and ψ⁡(Ct)∈ℝ5\psi(C_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{5} collects pool-level credit statistics,

ψ⁡(Ct)=(c¯,σc,cmin,cmax,ϕ^¯recent).\psi(C_{t})=\bigl(\bar{c},\;\sigma_{c},\;c_{\min},\;c_{\max},\;\bar{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{recent}}\bigr). (10)

Here, c¯\bar{c}, σc\sigma_{c}, cminc_{\min}, and cmaxc_{\max} denote the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum historical credit over the current pool, and ϕ^¯recent\bar{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{recent}} denotes the mean recent leave-one-out credit. The first two slots condition edits on observed task-level behavior and on the semantic composition of the assembled team. Writing χt∈{Warmup,Main}\chi_{t}\in\{\textsc{Warmup},\textsc{Main}\} for the training phase, the credit slot is retained but masked to zero during Warmup so early exploration does not depend on stale credit memory. A shared encoder maps oto_{t} to hth_{t}, an operation head produces a distribution over 𝒪\mathcal{O}, and a per-role head scores admissible removal targets using each role’s prompt embedding and local credit features. For Remove, with per-role score ξi​(ot)\xi_{i}(o_{t}) and admissible target set 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}, the target is sampled from the masked conditional

pθ​(zt=ri∣ωt=Remove,ot)=exp⁡(ξi​(ot))∑j∈𝒱texp⁡(ξj​(ot)).p_{\theta}(z_{t}{=}r_{i}\mid\omega_{t}{=}\textsc{Remove},o_{t})=\frac{\exp\!\bigl(\xi_{i}(o_{t})\bigr)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}\exp\!\bigl(\xi_{j}(o_{t})\bigr)}. (11)

Add has no controller-level target and creates a new card using the highest-EMA role selected inside ℰ\mathcal{E} as its anchor. The mask enforces the invariants from § 3.1, including phase-dependent constraints via χt\chi_{t}, protection flags bib_{i}, and minimum coverage requirements. We train πθ\pi_{\theta} with REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) using batch-normalized rewards and an EMA baseline.

Candidate Generator ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Given the controller’s action at=(ωt,zt)a_{t}=(\omega_{t},z_{t}), ℰ\mathcal{E} produces a schema-conforming, contract-checked candidate pool before scoring. For Add, ℰ\mathcal{E} uses a role editor anchored on the highest-EMA role to generate a typed card rnewr_{\text{new}} from task context, the current pool, credit summaries, and coverage diagnostics, and rejects candidates that violate the schema, over-concentrate dominant capability families, or near-duplicate existing prompts. For Remove, ℰ\mathcal{E} proposes deleting a role only when removal preserves all contracts, and for Noop it returns the current pool unchanged. The output is a candidate state (𝒫t′,Ct′)(\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{t},C^{\prime}_{t}) evaluated through FF and passed to Γ\Gamma.

Commitment Rule Γ\Gamma.

A candidate edit is committed only if it both satisfies the five contracts, enforced by the action mask and the constructor checks above, and improves the task score over the unedited pool. The score-side test uses RtR_{t} in Eq. 8 with phase-dependent thresholds controlled by χt\chi_{t}, kept conservative to filter single-task noise and prevent gradual drift from many small commits. If Γ\Gamma rejects a real edit, (𝒫t,Ct)(\mathcal{P}_{t},C_{t}) is restored exactly, while the controller is still updated using the observed RtR_{t}. Training loop in Algorithm 2 .

4 Experiments

Benchmarks and Metrics.

We evaluate on three benchmark families chosen to stress different structural demands and answer contracts. NaturalPlan (Zheng et al., 2024) mixes trip planning, calendar scheduling, and meeting planning, and we report both partial and exact task accuracy. For TableBench (Wu et al., 2025), we use the non-visual subset covering fact checking, numerical reasoning, and data analysis over text-only tables, scored as normalized single-line answer accuracy. For OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), we use the text-only English open-ended question subset covering competition mathematics and physics, scored with the official judge and string-matching fallback. Held-out split statistics and metric definitions are reported in Appendix B.

Baselines.

We compare Sero against six baselines spanning single-agent prompting, fixed workflows, static multi-agent graphs, frozen-pool orchestration, and random role evolution. CoT (Wei et al., 2022) is the single-call baseline, and SC@3 (Wang et al., 2022) uses self-consistency with k=3k=3. Workflow is a benchmark-specific hand-written linear decomposition. Static DAG MAS is a benchmark-specific hand-designed non-linear agent graph. Static Role Orchestration keeps Sero’s seed pool and the same retrieval-and-DAG inference pipeline but freezes the role pool. Random Role Evolution keeps the same edit space and role-card editor as Sero but replaces learned edit selection with uniform random actions. Taken together, these comparisons test whether any gains come mainly from stronger prompting, hand-designed decomposition, generic multi-agent structure, or specifically from learned contract-preserving role evolution. Exact prompts and graph definitions are reported in Appendix C.

Implementation Details.

We report results for GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2024), Gemini-2.5-flash-lite (Kilpatrick and Gleicher, 2025), and Qwen3-8b (Yang et al., 2025). Within each comparison block, the backbone is frozen; task text, role prompts, and inference messages are embedded by a frozen Jina Embeddings v2 sentence encoder (small, English) (Günther et al., 2023); and only a lightweight factorized MLP controller for role editing is trainable. Thus, observed differences primarily reflect coordination and adaptation rather than model scale. The controller architecture and implementation are detailed in Appendix D.1. Trainable variants share the same benchmark-specific training partition and are evaluated on the same held-out split as non-trainable baselines. Split statistics and dataset details are provided in Appendix B.1.

4.1 Main Results

Table 2 reports averages over three seeds, with seed-level breakdowns in Appendix E.1. Sero is the top method on every metric for GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-flash-lite, lifting the average score by +1.51+1.51 and +5.51+5.51 over the strongest baseline respectively, and remains best on OlympiadBench and TableBench under Qwen3-8b. These results show that credit-guided role evolution yields structural gains beyond what single-agent prompting, hand-written workflows, or frozen multi-agent graphs can supply, with the strongest lift on backbones that can exploit deeper multi-agent coordination. Qwen3-8b on NaturalPlan is the exception, where Static DAG MAS retains the lead and marks the scope limit when a smaller open model meets strictly format-constrained planning.

4.2 Framework Analysis

Hyperparameter Sensitivity.

Fig. 3 reports one-at-a-time sweeps of the specialist budget NspecN_{\mathrm{spec}}, credit-EMA momentum μ\mu, and collaboration rounds TT. Sero stays competitive across the swept range of every axis, though the optimum is benchmark dependent, with math and table benchmarks preferring more diverse specialist pools and lighter smoothing while NaturalPlan tolerates the opposite. The gains therefore do not hinge on a single point but track the per-benchmark trade-off between specialist coverage and format discipline.

Ablation Study.

Table 3 isolates each Sero component. The full method tops every metric, removing credit yields the largest drop (−13.22-13.22 on NP-E and −10.02-10.02 on NP-P), identifying credit as dominant since it jointly governs edit decisions and role orchestration. Protection, controller reward, and learned evolution add smaller, consistent lifts, while the three non-Sero baselines fall below every w/o ablation, indicating gains come from coupling learned role edits with credit-based feedback, rather than static structures or unguided role churn.

Active-Set Signatures.

Fig. 4 groups each evaluation instance by the family-level multiset of its active roles. A few dominant signatures capture most routing decisions on both backbones, and each signature keeps a stable Reasoning + Validation + Synthesis core while varying the specialist families around it. This reveals that Sero reuses a small library of coordination templates whose specialist mix is conditioned on task type rather than building a per-instance graph, consistent with gains tracking structured reuse over activation breadth.

Mechanism Analysis.

The dominant signatures in Fig. 4 establish that evaluation-time routing reuses a small set of stable templates rather than constructing per-instance idiosyncratic graphs. Table 4 adds the cost-accuracy view, where Sero matches Static DAG MAS in inference call count and adds only a modest token increase while improving the cross-backbone average score by +2.83+2.83 absolute, indicating that the gains come from learning reusable, benchmark-dependent coordination templates rather than from invoking more agents. Role-pool lifecycle statistics and routing breakdowns in Appendix E.2 and Appendix E.3.

Scaling Behavior.

Fig. 5 separates two scaling axes under Sero. Base-model scaling on Qwen3 (left) lifts all three benchmarks as the model grows from 1.71.7B to 3232B, so contract-preserving evolution keeps converting backbone capability into task score. Controller-width scaling on Gemini-2.5-flash-lite (right) is by contrast flat across hidden widths dhd_{h} from 6464 to 10241024. The gains therefore track backbone capacity rather than controller capacity, and a small contextual-bandit controller already suffices. Exact numbers in Appendix E.5.

5 Conclusion

We propose Sero, a framework realizing contract-preserving role evolution over a persistent role pool under five structural contracts. Sero recasts role-pool adaptation as guarded editing, in which candidate edits are proposed freely but committed only when they preserve every contract and improve the task objective. Extensive experiments on NaturalPlan, TableBench, and OlympiadBench across three diverse LLM backbones establish Sero’s superiority over advanced baselines.

Limitations

Sero is currently restricted to text-only benchmarks with automatically scorable outputs, and its seed role pool is hand-designed by capability family. Extending the framework to multimodal reasoning, multilingual settings, or domains with sparse or subjective rewards remains future work, as does a fully end-to-end accounting of training-time cost across larger backbones.

Appendix A Extended Related Work

A.1 Role-Based Multi-Agent Systems

Role-based LLM-agent systems decompose a task by assigning different prompts or personas to different model instances. CAMEL studies role-playing societies of agents (Li et al., 2023); MetaGPT turns software-development processes into coordinated agent roles (Hong et al., 2024); AutoGen provides a framework for programmable multi-agent conversation (Wu et al., 2023); and debate-style systems use multiple agents to expose and challenge intermediate reasoning (Du et al., 2024). These systems motivate Sero’s use of roles, but they generally keep the role set fixed within a run or rely on developer-specified decompositions. Sero instead treats the reusable role inventory as a state that can be edited under structural constraints.

A.2 Graph-Structured Agent Collaboration

Graph-structured agent methods focus on how agents communicate. GPTSwarm optimizes collaboration graphs over predefined components (Zhuge et al., 2024); G-Designer and AMAS construct task-adaptive graphs (Zhang et al., 2025b; Leong et al., 2025); ARG-Designer jointly chooses agent roles and communication links for a query (Li et al., 2026); SC-MAS assigns edge-level collaboration strategies and model choices (Zhao et al., 2026); GoAgent builds group-centric communication graphs (Chen et al., 2026); and TodyComm adapts communication across rounds (Fan et al., 2026). These approaches are closely related because Sero also rebuilds a DAG for each active team. The difference is that Sero makes graph construction dependent on typed role cards and persistent role-pool evolution, rather than only optimizing query-time communication structure or one-shot team composition.

A.3 Agent Pruning and Credit Assignment

Pruning and selection methods reduce the cost of multi-agent collaboration by removing unnecessary agents or links. AgentPrune learns spatial-temporal masks for economical communication pipelines (Zhang et al., 2025a); AgentDropout removes redundant agents or links across collaboration rounds (Wang et al., 2025); AGP jointly prunes agent quantity and communication topology (Li et al., 2025); and EIB-Learner analyzes how sparse and dense topologies propagate useful and erroneous information (Shen et al., 2025). Credit assignment provides complementary signals for estimating agent value, including difference rewards (Wolpert and Tumer, 2001), Shapley-style values (Shapley, 2016), and recent LLM-agent credit or contribution-guided optimization methods (Nagpal et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026). Sero uses credit for ranking, routing, and controller state, but prevents credit noise from directly deleting protected terminal roles, validators, or the last role covering a required capability family.

A.4 Dynamic Role and Prompt Evolution

Dynamic prompt and role systems aim to make multi-agent collaboration less dependent on hand-written decompositions. Dynamic role assignment selects suitable debate participants for role slots (Zhang et al., 2026); MetaGen rewrites query-conditioned role prompts and topologies at inference time (Wang et al., 2026); Multi-Agent Evolve studies self-play evolution of cooperative capabilities within a fixed proposer–solver–judge template (Chen et al., 2025); and ARG-Designer can choose agents from an extensible pool as part of graph construction (Li et al., 2026). Sero is closest to this family, but differs in how it treats adaptation: a candidate role-pool edit is not immediately trusted as a query-time assignment, prompt refinement, or graph decision. It must be a schema-valid role-card update, satisfy diversity and benchmark constraints, preserve the structural contracts, and improve observed task score before it becomes part of the persistent pool.

Appendix B Benchmark and Evaluation Details

B.1 Split and Subtask Statistics

Table 5 summarizes the training and held-out evaluation partitions used in all experiments. The training partition is reserved for trainable systems, and every method is evaluated on the same held-out test instances. For TableBench, the three task families aggregate the 17 non-visual question subtypes in the split. For OlympiadBench, the raw benchmark pool is sampled from two text-only English open-ended competition subset: OE_TO_maths_en_COMP (674 items) and OE_TO_physics_en_COMP (236 items). The effective split contains 897 available items rather than 910 because the loader applies an additional text-only guard and removes 13 entries that still reference visual material through words such as “figure”, “image”, or “shown below” (5 mathematics and 8 physics items). No further OlympiadBench item is removed by the split quality filter. The resulting available pool contains 669 mathematics and 228 physics items, from which we select 12/8 training examples and evaluate on the remaining 657/220 held-out examples.

B.2 Evaluation Metrics

For benchmark BB with held-out set 𝒟B={(xi,yi)}i=1NB\mathcal{D}_{B}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{B}} and per-instance score si=sxi​(y^i)∈[0,1]s_{i}=s_{x_{i}}(\hat{y}_{i})\in[0,1], the mean task score is

SB=1NB​∑i=1NBsi,S_{B}=\frac{1}{N_{B}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{B}}s_{i}, (12)

where y^i\hat{y}_{i} is the system’s parsed answer on task xix_{i} and sxi​(⋅)s_{x_{i}}(\cdot) is the benchmark-specific scorer. For a subtask group gg with held-out instances 𝒟B,g⊆𝒟B\mathcal{D}_{B,g}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{B}, the diagnostic score is

SB,g=1|𝒟B,g|​∑(xi,yi)∈𝒟B,gsi.S_{B,g}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{B,g}|}\sum_{(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathcal{D}_{B,g}}s_{i}. (13)

NaturalPlan.

NaturalPlan records two per-instance metrics, a partial score pi∈[0,1]p_{i}\in[0,1] and an exact score ei∈{0,1}e_{i}\in\{0,1\}. With NNP=|𝒟NP|N_{\mathrm{NP}}=|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{NP}}|, we report

PNP=1NNP​∑ipi,ENP=1NNP​∑iei.P_{\mathrm{NP}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{NP}}}\sum_{i}p_{i},\qquad E_{\mathrm{NP}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{NP}}}\sum_{i}e_{i}. (14)

For trip planning, the partial score is day-slot agreement. Let ci⋆​(t)c_{i}^{\star}(t) be the gold city assigned to day tt, TiT_{i} the total number of trip days, and 𝒵i\mathcal{Z}_{i} the set of non-empty parsed itinerary candidates extracted from the response. Each candidate z∈𝒵iz\in\mathcal{Z}_{i} induces a predicted day-city function c^i,z​(t)\hat{c}_{i,z}(t), and the trip partial score is

pitrip=maxz∈𝒵i1Ti∑t=1Ti[c^i,z(t)=ci⋆(t)].p_{i}^{\mathrm{trip}}=\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{i}}\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{c}_{i,z}(t)=c_{i}^{\star}(t)\right]. (15)

Trip exact accuracy follows the NaturalPlan flight-sequence parser rather than raw-string equality. Let Gi=((ci​1⋆,di​1⋆),…,(ci​Ki⋆,di​Ki⋆))G_{i}=((c_{i1}^{\star},d_{i1}^{\star}),\ldots,(c_{iK_{i}}^{\star},d_{iK_{i}}^{\star})) be the gold city-duration sequence from the benchmark fields. From a response, the parser extracts ordered flight statements, takes the first flight origin followed by each flight destination as the predicted city sequence (c~i​1,…,c~i​K~i)(\tilde{c}_{i1},\ldots,\tilde{c}_{i\tilde{K}_{i}}), and infers inclusive stay lengths from the parsed flight days. If τ~i​0=1\tilde{\tau}_{i0}=1, τ~i​K~i\tilde{\tau}_{i\tilde{K}_{i}} is the end day of the final parsed visit range, and τ~i​1,…,τ~i,K~i−1\tilde{\tau}_{i1},\ldots,\tilde{\tau}_{i,\tilde{K}_{i}-1} are the extracted flight days, then

d~i​k=τ~i​k−τ~i,k−1+1,k=1,…,K~i.\tilde{d}_{ik}=\tilde{\tau}_{ik}-\tilde{\tau}_{i,k-1}+1,\qquad k=1,\ldots,\tilde{K}_{i}. (16)

The trip exact score is therefore

eitrip=[K~i≥Ki∧⋀k=1Ki((c~i​k,d~i​k)=(ci​k⋆,di​k⋆))],e_{i}^{\mathrm{trip}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\tilde{K}_{i}\geq K_{i}\;\land\;\bigwedge_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\bigl((\tilde{c}_{ik},\tilde{d}_{ik})=(c_{ik}^{\star},d_{ik}^{\star})\bigr)\right], (17)

so any first mismatch in the ordered city-duration prefix gives zero exact credit.

For meeting planning, let Mi⋆M_{i}^{\star} be the number of valid meetings in the gold route, MipartialM_{i}^{\mathrm{partial}} the number of independently valid meetings counted by the permissive evaluator, and MistrictM_{i}^{\mathrm{strict}} the strict valid-meeting count under break-on-first-error execution. The scores are

pimeet\displaystyle p_{i}^{\mathrm{meet}} =min⁡(1,MipartialMi⋆),\displaystyle=\min\!\left(1,\frac{M_{i}^{\mathrm{partial}}}{M_{i}^{\star}}\right), (18)
eimeet\displaystyle e_{i}^{\mathrm{meet}} =[Mistrict=Mi⋆].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[M_{i}^{\mathrm{strict}}=M_{i}^{\star}\right].

The permissive evaluator skips invalid steps but advances time using the response’s stated durations so later meetings can still receive credit. The strict evaluator validates travel, waits, meeting windows, and stated times, and stops at the first error. Calendar scheduling is the degenerate case where partial and exact coincide,

pical=eical=[d^i=di⋆∧s^i=si⋆∧t^i=ti⋆],p_{i}^{\mathrm{cal}}=e_{i}^{\mathrm{cal}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{d}_{i}=d_{i}^{\star}\land\hat{s}_{i}=s_{i}^{\star}\land\hat{t}_{i}=t_{i}^{\star}\right], (19)

with di⋆,si⋆,ti⋆d_{i}^{\star},s_{i}^{\star},t_{i}^{\star} the gold day, start time, and end time, and d^i,s^i,t^i\hat{d}_{i},\hat{s}_{i},\hat{t}_{i} their predicted counterparts after time normalization.

TableBench.

Each item receives lenient exact accuracy,

siTB=[M⁡(ν⁡(a^i),ν⁡(ai⋆))],s_{i}^{\mathrm{TB}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[M\bigl(\nu(\hat{a}_{i}),\nu(a_{i}^{\star})\bigr)\right], (20)

where a^i\hat{a}_{i} and ai⋆a_{i}^{\star} are the predicted and gold answers, ν\nu denotes answer normalization, and MM is exact string match except for supported numeric cases. For tolerance-enabled statistical subtypes,

M(v^,v)=[|v^−v|max⁡(|v|,ϵ)≤0.1],M(\hat{v},v)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\frac{|\hat{v}-v|}{\max(|v|,\epsilon)}\leq 0.1\right], (21)

with v^\hat{v} and vv the predicted and gold numeric values and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 a small constant guarding against division by zero.

OlympiadBench.

Let J⁡(a^,a⋆)J(\hat{a},a^{\star}) be the OlympiadBench judge, with string matching as a fallback. The benchmark contributes one scalar score per item. For single-answer items, this score is binary,

siOB=[J⁡(a^i,ai⋆)],s_{i}^{\mathrm{OB}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[J(\hat{a}_{i},a_{i}^{\star})\right], (22)

where a^i\hat{a}_{i} and ai⋆a_{i}^{\star} are the predicted and gold answers. For multi-answer items, the scorer first asks the judge to match the full predicted answer against the full gold answer; if this full-set check fails, it splits both sides into answer components and greedily matches each gold component to at most one predicted component. With gold components Ai⋆={ai​1⋆,…,ai​K⋆}A_{i}^{\star}=\{a_{i1}^{\star},\ldots,a_{iK}^{\star}\}, predicted components A^i={a^i​1,…,a^i​L}\hat{A}_{i}=\{\hat{a}_{i1},\ldots,\hat{a}_{iL}\}, and ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} denoting the resulting one-to-one set of matched index pairs, the reported item score is

siOB=1K​∑(k,j)∈ℳi[J⁡(a^i​j,ai​k⋆)].s_{i}^{\mathrm{OB}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{(k,j)\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[J(\hat{a}_{ij},a_{ik}^{\star})\right]. (23)

Appendix C Baseline Implementations

This appendix defines the comparison systems used in the experiments. All baselines are run on the same loaded tasks, benchmark adapters, canonical answer extractors, and scoring functions as Sero. Let xix_{i} denote a task, FbF_{b} the benchmark-specific answer extractor, and SbS_{b} the scorer. For a multi-agent baseline with role cards RbR_{b}, directed message edges EbE_{b}, and terminal role tbt_{b}, execution is a topological pass over a fixed graph, with Ur={mu:(u,r)∈Eb}U_{r}=\{m_{u}:(u,r)\in E_{b}\}, mr=fθ​(πr,xi,Ur)m_{r}=f_{\theta}(\pi_{r},x_{i},U_{r}), and a^i=Fb​(mtb)\hat{a}_{i}=F_{b}(m_{t_{b}}). where πr\pi_{r} is the system prompt stored in role card rr. The baselines differ only in how the role set and graph are chosen, and in whether the role pool is allowed to change. Detailed prompt bundles for the multi-agent baselines appear in §§ C.3, C.4 and D.3.

C.1 Overview

This subsection summarizes what each baseline fixes or learns and the contribution it isolates. Detailed implementations are in §§ C.2, C.3, C.4, C.5 and C.6.

  • •

    CoT. A single deterministic response from the base model at temperature 00 using the same benchmark-specific single-agent prompt as Sero, which measures strong single-agent prompting without multi-agent structure.

  • •

    SC@3. Three temperature-0.70.7 samples followed by majority vote over canonical extracted answers, which tests whether simple sampling can substitute for role orchestration.

  • •

    Workflow. A benchmark-specific hand-written linear decomposition with no credit, retrieval, DAG construction, or evolution, which controls for the contribution of any sequentially-decomposed pipeline regardless of structure.

  • •

    Static DAG MAS. A benchmark-specific hand-designed non-linear role graph with a fixed topology and fixed terminal aggregator, which tests whether expert-designed topology alone can explain the performance attributed to learned coordination.

  • •

    Static Role Orchestration. Sero’s seed pool combined with the same retrieval, credit-ranked DAG execution, aggregation, and validator repair pipeline, but with role-pool evolution disabled, which isolates the value of learned role-pool evolution beyond the rest of the inference pipeline.

  • •

    Random Role Evolution. The same edit space and role-card editor as Sero, but edit operations are sampled uniformly at random instead of from the learned controller and are committed without a score gate, which tests whether the controller and commitment rule add value beyond unconstrained exploration.

  • •

    Sero (Ours). The learned guarded controller, constrained role editor, score-gated commitment, and frozen test-time pool, evaluated under the same inference operator as the static-pool baselines.

C.2 Single-Agent Baselines

CoT (Wei et al., 2022) is the deterministic one-call baseline. For benchmark bb, let pbSAp_{b}^{\mathrm{SA}} denote the benchmark-specific single-agent system prompt used throughout the evaluation protocol. The evaluator queries the base model once with temperature T=0T=0:

yi=fθ​(pbSA,xi,T=0),a^i=Fb​(yi).y_{i}=f_{\theta}(p_{b}^{\mathrm{SA}},x_{i};T=0),\qquad\hat{a}_{i}=F_{b}(y_{i}).

SC@3 (Wang et al., 2022) keeps the same prompt but samples three independent responses at temperature 0.70.7, extracts a canonical answer from each response, and returns the majority answer:

yi(j)\displaystyle y_{i}^{(j)} ∼fθ(pbSA,xi;T=0.7),j=1,2,3,\displaystyle\sim f_{\theta}(p_{b}^{\mathrm{SA}},x_{i};T=0.7),\qquad j=1,2,3,
zi(j)\displaystyle z_{i}^{(j)} =Fb​(yi(j)),\displaystyle=F_{b}(y_{i}^{(j)}),
a^i\displaystyle\hat{a}_{i} =arg​maxz∈{zi(1),zi(2),zi(3)}z≠∅∑j=13[zi(j)=z].\displaystyle=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\{z_{i}^{(1)},z_{i}^{(2)},z_{i}^{(3)}\}\\ z\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\sum_{j=1}^{3}\mathbf{1}\!\left[z_{i}^{(j)}=z\right].

Ties in this vote are resolved by the earliest sampled response. If every response fails canonical extraction, SC@3 scores the first sampled response. This makes the comparison depend on the same answer normalization as Sero, rather than on free-form text similarity.

C.3 Workflow Baselines

Workflow is a hand-written sequential multi-agent baseline. For each supported benchmark, the baseline uses a fixed ordered list of role cards and a single terminal card. The graph is always a chain, r1→r2→⋯→rK=tbr_{1}\rightarrow r_{2}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow r_{K}=t_{b}, so execution reduces to mr1=fθ​(πr1,xi)m_{r_{1}}=f_{\theta}(\pi_{r_{1}},x_{i}) and mrk=fθ​(πrk,xi,mrk−1)m_{r_{k}}=f_{\theta}(\pi_{r_{k}},x_{i},m_{r_{k-1}}) for k=2,…,Kk=2,\ldots,K. This baseline only passes messages and calls agents. It does not use the adaptive retrieval module, the learned controller, credit computation, role selection, or role-pool evolution.

Figs. 6–8 give the full Workflow specification for NaturalPlan: the topology, role-card fields, and exact system-prompt content of every role in the chain. OlympiadBench uses an analogous problem decomposer →\to solution strategist →\to verification expert →\to answer synthesizer chain with mathematics and physics specialists in place of trip / calendar / meeting roles, and TableBench follows an analogous table parser →\to evidence selector →\to table solver →\to answer auditor →\to final formatter chain over tabular questions.

C.4 Static DAG MAS Baselines

Static DAG MAS is a hand-designed non-linear multi-agent baseline. Each benchmark receives a dedicated role set, a fixed edge set, and a fixed terminal role. Unlike Workflow, a role may receive several upstream messages, and independent branches are executed in parallel levels. If L1,…,LHL_{1},\ldots,L_{H} are the resulting topological levels, then for each level

Ur\displaystyle U_{r} ={mu:(u,r)∈Eb},\displaystyle=\{m_{u}:(u,r)\in E_{b}\},
mr\displaystyle m_{r} =fθ(πr,xi,Ur),r∈Lh.\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(\pi_{r},x_{i},U_{r}),\qquad r\in L_{h}.

The terminal role then receives its predecessors and produces the final answer. This baseline has no learned controller, no credit ranking, no retrieval over a seed pool, and no role-pool edits.

Figs. 9–12 give the full Static DAG specification for NaturalPlan: the parallel trip / calendar / meeting specialist branches, the cross-task auditor, and the protected format finalizer. OlympiadBench uses a concept identifier →\to algebraic / intuitive solver branches →\to cross-checker →\to answer extractor DAG, and TableBench uses a question schema mapper →\to evidence retriever →\to numerical / lookup specialist branches →\to arithmetic auditor →\to answer-auditor synthesizer →\to final formatter DAG with the parser-facing format enforced by the protected terminal.

C.5 Static Role Orchestration

Static Role Orchestration is the frozen seed-pool variant of Sero, not the expert static graph above: it uses Sero’s benchmark seed role pool and the same retrieval-and-DAG inference engine as Sero. The only disabled component is role-pool evolution. Formally, if 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} is the seed pool, then

𝒫i+1\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{i+1} =𝒫i=𝒫0,\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{i}=\mathcal{P}_{0},
Ai\displaystyle A_{i} =Retrieve⁡(xi,𝒫0),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Retrieve}(x_{i},\mathcal{P}_{0}),
Gi\displaystyle G_{i} =DAG⁡(Ai).\displaystyle=\operatorname{DAG}(A_{i}).

The static seed roles are still selected, ordered, aggregated, and optionally repaired by the same inference machinery as Sero, using current-task bootstrap signals to order the DAG but without updating fast-credit state during evaluation. No Add, Remove, or Noop action can alter the pool.

C.6 Random Role Evolution

Random Role Evolution isolates whether performance gains can be explained by role-pool perturbation alone. It starts from the same seed pool as Sero and uses the same role-card editor, schema validation, maximum pool size PmaxP_{\max}, protected-role removal constraint, and frozen evaluation operator. Its only difference from Sero’s learned evolution stage is that edit choices are sampled uniformly and are never accepted or rejected by a before–after score comparison. For training task xix_{i} and current pool 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i},

𝒪\displaystyle\mathcal{O} ={Add,Remove,Noop},\displaystyle=\{\textsc{Add},\textsc{Remove},\textsc{Noop}\},
ωi\displaystyle\omega_{i} ∼Unif⁡(𝒪),\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal{O}),
ρi\displaystyle\rho_{i} ∼Unif(𝒫i)if ωi≠Noop,\displaystyle\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathcal{P}_{i})\quad\text{if }\omega_{i}\neq\textsc{Noop},
𝒫i+1\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{i+1} =U⁡(𝒫i,ωi,ρi,xi).\displaystyle=U(\mathcal{P}_{i},\omega_{i},\rho_{i};x_{i}).

Here ρi\rho_{i} denotes the sampled target role and UU denotes the random role-pool update: Remove deletes ρi\rho_{i} unless doing so would remove a protected role or empty the pool, Add appends a schema-valid role proposed from the current task context and the role with highest historical EMA credit when |𝒫i|<Pmax|\mathcal{P}_{i}|<P_{\max}, and Noop leaves the pool unchanged. Scores observed on the training tasks are recorded only for analysis, not for edit commitment. After the random evolution pass, the final pool is frozen and evaluated with the same retrieval, bootstrap credit-ranked DAG construction, aggregation, and validator-repair procedure used for Sero.

Appendix D Sero Training Details

This section documents the controller specification, the hyperparameter profiles, the seed role cards, the training strategy, the credit-ranked DAG construction routine, and the full training step used in the experiments.

D.1 Controller Details

The controller is the only trainable neural component in Sero. Intuitively, it reads three pieces of state: how the current task attempt interacted with the benchmark, which roles were active in that attempt, and how healthy the current role pool looks according to the five credit statistics in Eq. 10. Under the 512-dimensional encoder used in these experiments, these signals form a 1029-dimensional state vector. A shared two-layer MLP with hidden size 256 maps this vector to a latent state. One head chooses the edit type from {Add,Remove,Noop}\{\textsc{Add},\textsc{Remove},\textsc{Noop}\}, while a second conditional head scores admissible target roles using the latent state, a learned 64-dimensional operation embedding, a projected role embedding, and two local credit features: the role’s historical EMA credit and recent leave-one-out credit. We train this policy with REINFORCE using batch-normalized rewards, an EMA baseline, and entropy regularization, while keeping both the task backbone and the text encoder frozen.

D.2 Hyperparameters

The experiments use a small family of closely related profiles rather than a single universal setting. Table 6 lists the reference profile for Qwen-3-8b together with the alternative profile used for GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-flash-lite. Main comparisons average runs over seeds 42, 43, and 44. Hyperparameter sensitivity, ablation, and controller-scaling experiments use seed 44, while base-model scaling uses seed 43. Unless a dedicated sensitivity analysis explicitly varies a given factor, both the hyperparameter-sensitivity experiments and the ablation experiments inherit the same settings as the corresponding main experiment. Scaling experiments follow the corresponding main-experiment model–benchmark profile, except that the Qwen3 model-size sweep uses the GPT-4o-mini / Gemini profile in Table 6 for all Qwen3 sizes to isolate backbone scale under a fixed training configuration.

D.3 Seed Roles

The main three-benchmark setting starts from a 10-role cross-task NaturalPlan pool, a 7-role TableBench pool, and a 7-role OlympiadBench pool. The highlighted blocks below reproduce the current seed role cards, including role type, protection flag, capability family, communication protocol, and the exact system-prompt line structure. Code-level role_type values ’router’, ’specialist’, ’validator’, and ’aggregator’ correspond respectively to the canonical role types 𝖲𝖾𝗍𝗎𝗉\mathsf{Setup}, 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Spec}, 𝖵𝖺𝗅\mathsf{Val}, and 𝖠𝗀𝗀\mathsf{Agg} from § 3.1. The single-column prompt blocks below are presented in the order Combined NaturalPlan, TableBench, and OlympiadBench.

Figs. 13–18 show the ten role cards of the NaturalPlan seed pool: a task-and-contract parser, eight domain specialists covering trip, calendar, and meeting subtasks plus a cross-task constraint validator, and a protected aggregator that enforces the parser-facing final format. Figs. 19 and 20 show the seven role cards of the OlympiadBench seed pool: symbolic and structural solvers, a problem formalizer, a technique scout, a physics frame analyst, a completeness auditor, and a protected answer synthesizer. The TableBench seed pool follows the same router-specialist-validator-aggregator structure with seven roles spanning schema mapping, evidence retrieval, numerical reasoning, data-analysis interpretation, fact checking, an answer verifier, and a protected aggregator.

D.4 Training Strategy

Training is one-edit-per-task policy learning over a committed role pool. Given task xix_{i} and committed state (𝒫i,Ci)(\mathcal{P}_{i},C_{i}), the inference operator first produces a pre-edit answer y^i\hat{y}_{i}, score si−=sxi​(y^i)s_{i}^{-}=s_{x_{i}}(\hat{y}_{i}), and controller observation oio_{i}. The controller then samples an edit action ai=(ωi,zi)a_{i}=(\omega_{i},z_{i}) with ωi∈𝒪={Add,Remove,Noop}\omega_{i}\in\mathcal{O}=\{\textsc{Add},\textsc{Remove},\textsc{Noop}\}, where ziz_{i} is a target role when the action requires one. The candidate generator ℰ\mathcal{E} proposes a candidate state (𝒫~i,C~i)(\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{i},\widetilde{C}_{i}), and the same task is re-evaluated under this candidate state to produce a post-edit score si+s_{i}^{+}. The episode reward is Ri=0R_{i}=0 for Noop or an unchanged candidate, and Ri=si+−si−R_{i}=s_{i}^{+}-s_{i}^{-} otherwise.

The training schedule has a warmup phase followed by a main phase. Warmup omits credit-state features from the controller input and disables removal, so the pool can only add roles or stay unchanged. In warmup, non-NaturalPlan real edits are committed when they are non-harmful (Ri≥0R_{i}\geq 0); in the main phase, committed edits must be strictly improving (Ri>0R_{i}>0). NaturalPlan uses strict add acceptance throughout, so newly proposed roles are committed only when they improve the task score. Rejected real edits restore the pre-edit credit state exactly, which prevents tentative fast-credit updates from leaking into later episodes.

Each training batch applies REINFORCE with batch-normalized rewards, an exponential-moving-average baseline, and operation-head entropy regularization; the batch size follows the active profile in Table 6. If R^i\hat{R}_{i} denotes the batch-normalized reward and bb the EMA baseline, the policy objective is

maxθ⁡1B​∑i=1B(R^i−b)​log⁡πθ​(ai∣oi)+β​ℋ​(πθop),\max_{\theta}\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}(\hat{R}_{i}-b)\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid o_{i})+\beta\,\mathcal{H}(\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{op}}),

with Adam optimization and gradient clipping. Precise leave-one-out credit is refreshed periodically once the pool has reached the minimum size specified by the active profile in Table 6; each refresh samples up to three training tasks and updates the historical credit state role by role.

Before an edit can be committed, the trainer also enforces the structural constraints used in the main system: pool-size bounds, protected-role removal blocking, seed-family coverage preservation, validator-count minima under the reserved validator pass, rejection of newly generated validator roles when the reserved validator pass is enabled, and diversity-based rejection for dominant-family or near-duplicate additions. During the main phase, training stops early if the committed pool stays unchanged for more than 85% of the most recent 24 main-phase episodes after at least one full main-phase window.

D.5 Credit-Ranked DAG Construction

This subsection makes explicit the graph-construction routine used inside the inference operator. Given the retrieved non-terminal set Bt=At∖{ragg}B_{t}=A_{t}\setminus\{r_{\mathrm{agg}}\}, the procedure first imposes the stage-aware total order from Eq. 7. Setup roles are therefore placed before specialist roles, validators are delayed until after specialist reasoning, and roles within the same stage are ordered by decreasing current fast credit with a deterministic index tie-breaker. In the reported experiments, when degree caps are not specified externally, the routine uses bout=max⁡(1,min⁡(2,n−1))b_{\mathrm{out}}=\max(1,\min(2,n-1)) and bin=max⁡(1,⌊n/2⌋)b_{\mathrm{in}}=\max(1,\lfloor n/2\rfloor) for n=|Bt|n=|B_{t}|.

Edges are then added only from earlier to later roles in this ordered list, subject to the out-degree budget of the source and the in-degree budget of the target. This forward orientation makes the intermediate communication graph acyclic by construction, while the final edges from every non-terminal role to raggr_{\mathrm{agg}} add a single terminal sink that preserves aggregator observability. The resulting graph is finally decomposed into dependency levels: all roles in one level have no unmet predecessor in BtB_{t} and can be invoked in parallel under the same upstream-message semantics used by FF.

D.6 Training Loop

For reference, Algorithm 2 states one full training step end-to-end, combining the pre-edit rollout, observation construction, candidate generation, and score-gated commitment described above.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results and Mechanism Analyses

This appendix reports the seed-level results and supplementary mechanism analyses referenced in the main experimental section. All analyses are derived from the original training and evaluation runs without additional model queries.

E.1 Seed-Level Detailed Results

Table 7 reports the seed-level results underlying the main averaged table. For NaturalPlan, each seed reports partial (P) and exact (E) accuracy; OlympiadBench and TableBench report task score. All entries are percentages. Best and second-best per column within each backbone block.

E.2 Role-Pool Evolution

Role Lifecycle Statistics.

Table 8 tracks role-pool evolution by model, benchmark, and seed, jointly characterizing whether evolution produces durable specialists rather than merely enlarging the pool.

The pattern is benchmark- and backbone-dependent. NaturalPlan keeps the seed pool nearly intact under Gemini and GPT-4o-mini, OlympiadBench retains most added roles for downstream use, and TableBench is mixed with some additions going unused at evaluation time. Role evolution therefore behaves as a selective mechanism whose intensity is benchmark- and backbone-conditioned rather than uniformly active.

Case Study of Role Lifecycle Over Training.

Fig. 21 visualizes a representative Sero trajectory for Gemini-2.5-flash-lite on OlympiadBench, tracing structural interventions, role lifecycle states, and the family-level composition of active roles over training. The figure complements Table 8 by showing when pool revisions occur and whether the revised roles subsequently enter the inference topology.

E.3 Inference-Time Orchestration

Evaluation Active-Set Diversity.

Table 9 measures evaluation-time routing diversity through the number of distinct active sets, their entropy and Simpson concentration, the mean active-role count, and the unused-role ratio.

Routing diversity is strongest on OlympiadBench (hundreds of distinct active sets, near-maximal Simpson scores) and weakest on NaturalPlan, consistent with the latter’s stricter output requirements and more repetitive subtask structure. TableBench is intermediate but backbone-dependent, with GPT-4o-mini showing more active-set diversity than Gemini-2.5-flash-lite and Qwen3-8b cycling through a small but nontrivial family of configurations. The pattern is more consistent with task-conditioned routing than with stochastic variation alone.

Task-Conditioned Role Activation.

Figs. 22 and 23 test whether active-role variation is task-conditioned. Rows are subject-level task groups, columns are interpretable specialist roles, and each cell is the fraction of instances in a group that activate the role. The question is whether routing collapses to a universal role set or varies with task structure.

In both backbones, specialist usage concentrates by subject group rather than spreading uniformly, arguing against a universal role set or noisy switching. GPT-4o-mini shows richer subject-level differentiation, consistent with its larger number of unique active sets in Table 9, while Qwen3-8b retains task-conditioned specialization despite a smaller active team. The gains on OlympiadBench and TableBench therefore plausibly arise from selecting a better-matched specialist subset rather than from activating more roles.

The signature-level companion appears in the main text (Fig. 4). Together with the heatmaps, the picture is one of reusable yet conditionally adaptive routing rather than per-instance idiosyncratic graphs, clearest on OlympiadBench where adaptive routing yields the strongest gains in the main results.

E.4 Credit and Topology Alignment

Credit / DAG Alignment.

Table 10 tests whether Sero’s credit and topology mechanisms leave measurable signatures in the learned pool through three statistics, the correlation between credit and evaluation-time selection frequency, the pre-credit of removed roles, and the average credit of early versus late DAG positions.

Early-DAG credit usually exceeds late-DAG credit, consistent with the intended credit-ranked ordering of the inference graph. Credit-usage correlation is mixed in sign, which we interpret cautiously since roles can receive high credit through occasional high-leverage use without being most-frequently selected. The non-trivial pre-credit values observed for some removed roles indicate that removal reflects redundancy and pool restructuring rather than elimination of the globally weakest role.

Together, these analyses provide convergent evidence about Sero’s behavior. Pools evolve through persistent, reusable revisions, evaluation routing remains task-conditioned rather than collapsing to a single configuration, and learned credit aligns with the intended inference ordering.

E.5 Scaling Behavior

Tables 12 and 12 list the exact per-benchmark scores behind the curves in Fig. 5.
